The foot pads are wide enough that you don't slip off and the padded handlebars are great in case you topple to one side and accidentally bonk yourself in the face. (Hey, it happens!)

This stick is for beginners that are just learning. It takes about 2 days for a child to learn to pogo, especially if they are tall or longer-legged. Start on a very flat surface (not a slanted driveway) and encourage them to be patient as they learn how to balance on it. And once you learn, you never forget! But don't try it, dad - this pogo smashes pretty flat if an adult tries to use it because it's only rated to 80 pounds! (Might handle 90 lbs okay.) Soon they'll be able to do several bounces in a row and, before you're completely comfortable with the idea, they'll be taking massive leaps on the thing, galloping down the cul-de-sac!

Incredibly fun outdoor toy in a bright color that helps you spot it so you don't run it over if it's left out in the driveway!

I was fortunate to receive this product at a slight discount (not free) so that I could try it, use it, abuse it and determine if it is worth spending your hard-earned money on. If it doesn’t work, I will tell you. I hope my honesty helps you to make the best buying decision for your family!

Thames & Kosmos Forces & Interactions: Middle School Classroom Kit | NGSS-Aligned for Physics & Engineering Classes| Teacher Guide & Lesson Plans | Durable, Timed for Classroom Use, Includes Storage I generally love Thames and Kosovo’s products. This is a classroom physics kit. There are enough pieces to build several cars at once, but some experiments can only be done one at a time. For me that is fine since I am using this with homeschooling several kids, but for a small classroom, I can see students wanting to make their own. I am also not sure there are enough pieces to build more than one ramp. The snap pieces can be hard to remove especially for smaller finger, there is one connector puller included. For bigger groups of students I would have liked more of the pullers (looks a bit like the Lego splitter tool) You will need to provide weights for one experiment and batteries for the power module. I used slightly stronger nylon cord for my bucket pulls. It comes with magnets, wires, cord, nails, a cheep compass, and paper clips. Most of the odds and ends I just used my own and left the nails etc in the bucket.
There is a nice top divided tray to store the tinier pieces, and the bottom bin I left filled with the large pieces. The top of the storage box is dimpled to allow connecting the (not Lego) plastic building blocks to it. My kids had fun and easily figured out how to build onto any experiment we tried.
My one and biggest complaint with the kit is the magnet and iron filing board. None of the magnets work. They appear to have either been super heated or smacked around enough to unalign or weaken the magnet. I have a collection of bar magnets and rare earth magnets so I replaced the included magnets with my own. Most science teachers I know have collections of magnets so overall not a big issue. The clear iron filing board designed to show magnetic fields was a bust though. It’s not that the filings didn’t align, but that there were so few filings inside to show anything to begin with. I have a board I bought from a science teaching supply store and it has enough filings to demonstrate the magnetic field. This one was meh at best.
Because it does allow for multiple fun interactive classroom experiments I am rating this four stars. The spiral teaching book was great with Detailed instructions for building, and alignment guides (this assumes a knowledge of the material on the teacher’s part). The plastic technic like pieces were easy to use and fun for the kids. It was in the magnetism and wires and accessories that fell short of expectation. My Dad was a physicist (and MD) and I have a background in Physics as well, I had no trouble explaining what was going on to my kids, but this does not have answers to the questions because it assumes teacher knows answers, and how to relate NGSS Standards. Booklet includes lesson plan with target student age, time to teach, and any any materials needed. It is a great classroom kit, or group science instruction kit. Just keep in mind it’s target is classroom supplementary instruction, not home so kit is not designed to be a done by a kid on their own following a visually interesting book. (The spiral is pretty standard for teacher lesson books)
text_fidelity_b: Thames & Kosmos Forces & Interactions: Middle School Classroom Kit | NGSS-Aligned for Physics & Engineering Classes| Teacher Guide & Lesson Plans | Durable, Timed for Classroom Use, Includes Storage

text_fidelity_a:
Disney Hedbanz, 2nd Edition Picture-Guessing Family Board Game, for Adults and Kids Ages 7 and up (Styles May Vary) Got this for adults in family to play. 2 to 6 people play. No one had played before so we were learning strategies as we played. The only time limit is the one minute timer each person has in front of them when it is their turn to ask questions.

To start, a plastic adjustable headband apparatus is given to each player; maximun of six players. Tokens are passed out, 3 per person, one card is dealt to each person that is kept face down and not read; each player takes their one card and place it in the headband on their head so it faces out towards the other players. Do not have mirrors or reflective items nearby so no one can accidentally see their card. If a player leaves the table for a moment, they remove the card and place it face down on the table and return the card to the headband when they return, being careful not to read the card. In addition, a card of helpful questions is passed out to each player to help them ask meaningful questions to get critical answers so they can correctly guess who/what they are on their card.

Rules say the tallest person starts the game, but you have the freedom to start it in any way and play continues to the left. It is also extremely helpful to have a sheet of paper with pen or pencil so you can record answers to the questions you ask. It is hard to remember what questions you previously asked and valuable time is wasted if you are repeating questions that were already answered. We also learned great questions to ask as each player asked their own questions. The players answer with "I don't know", Yes, No, Could be, according to their knowledge of the question. Try to think before you answer and be sure you know the answer because that is critical to the player getting the correct information.

We played this game a lot and got better with each game as we learned how to ask very "to the point" questions. For instance, to start the game, you want to find out if you are a person (George Washington), place (the Great Wall of China) , or thing (jalapeno), (3 separate questions) and each time the other players will answer you with Yes, No, Could Be or Don't know. If you are a person, are you alive or dead? are you fictional (James Bond) or real (John Travolta); am I female or male; am I old or young, etc. The little hint cards do not give you all these options; you have to figure out how to ask your questions in a meaningful way. Each person asks questions until the sand in the timer runs out and play passes to the next person to the left. Keep going around the table until someone guesses their card correctly, and they win and surrender one token. A new round with new cards is started. Rounds are played until someone wins the most rounds and all their tokens surrendered.

You can surrender your card and get a new card and be penalized by receiving an additional token from "the bank" if your questioning is not getting you anywhere, or just start over from the beginning with your questioning because you may have misunderstood an answer that is leading you in the wrong direction. But we usually stuck it out and re-asked questions to find the correct path.

It is a very challenging game; you must be able to think out your progression of questions to reach a conclusion before anyone else. The first player to surrender all their tokens wins the game. The more we played, the better we got at asking questions and the faster we could complete a game, although it could be as long as 45 minutes. A very lively and intriguing game and highly recommended. It could be frustrating but keep a cool head and focus on "how" to ask critical questions. We will play it at all future get togethers and I can't wait until we do.
text_fidelity_b: Disney Hedbanz, 2nd Edition Picture-Guessing Family Board Game, for Adults and Kids Ages 7 and up (Styles May Vary)

That said, these EZ BioResearch Pre-poured Agar plates worked great for my child's science experiment. Three AAA batteries are needed to power the drill according to the instruction manual, and two AAA batteries are needed for the train engine for the sound and light. The wheels roll smoothly and securely, and it is easy to connect the three sections of the train together, so it is a good toy not just a building activity. text_fidelity_a: Air Hogs - Supernova, Gravity Defying Hand-Controlled Flying Orb, for Ages 8 and Up Still learning!!  This has had our house in a happy uproar since we got it!  After multiple readings of directions and many try outs we think we kind of have a handle on the basics but doing any tricks are an accidental result only.  Batteries are already in this.  Everything for power is concentrated in the center of this orb.  It comes w/USB to charge through our computer.  There is a tiny, tiny white slide tab in center by batteries that you move to turn this on.  Immediately (if charged) the center ball light will come on and flash colors.  When charging or a problem, the ball light will flash red only.  This is a fairly fragile  plastic caged flyer.  It doesn't weigh a lot because it has to keep it's self flying + hovering with 4 little sets of plastic blades that rotate (think fan blades).  Four extra blades come with this. Inside the orb besides the power center and the blades are sensors that will cause the orb to change directions when they are blocked in any way. To start, you have it on and slowly let it drop out of yr hands, it will drop and start hovering before it actually hits the floor(the sensors realize there is something in the way). After it starts hovering low over floor you get a hand(s) underneath and just start raising it and moving it all over the place by using yr hands to block the sensors...All the while, center light is flashing colors and the orb is making this noise..lol, between a whine & buzz and you find yrself almost running around the room trying to control this thing!  It will go up to the ceiling and then you have to figure out how to get a hand up to control it!  We don't dare take it outside to do, afraid it wouldn't come back!  This has fallen to the floor several times and not broken but, it is something you should take care with.  A lot of great accidental exercise and laughs!  Not for little children to use but they will love the show
text_fidelity_b: Air Hogs - Supernova, Gravity Defying Hand-Controlled Flying Orb, for Ages 8 and Up

text_fidelity_a:
CGE Czech Games Edition Thats A Question Excellent party game from the makers of Codenames. If you've played Codenames, then you know that is a fantastic party game, but that it requires the right group - a slow or domineering player can often mean that everyone is standing around staring at the board for an hour while they dole out perfectly configured clues. It's a fun game, but it requires the right group. That's a Question is a party game that can be played by absolutely anyone, and that, in my opinion, makes it almost a superior game.

In That's a Question!, players use cards to ask A/B style "would you rather" questions in which players attempt to guess the outcome. Based on the results, you move your pawn along the track.

The rulebook is well-written and funny, and is aware that this game is a little bit weird - attempting to give a theme to a basic Q&A style game, but it works. Of course, the game is not perfect. You are limited to only asking three different main questions, although the game does provide a wide variation of answers. There are also point modification questions which allow you to muddy up the scoring in your favor. Ultimately, the scoring was the part of the game that we found most cumbersome, and the modifiers didn't help that, simply adding a little more chaos. Scoring is also modified based on how many players are playing; as this was clearly designed as a 5-6 player game, a 4-player game has a few modifications, and the 3-player game has a fairly substantial number of scoring modifications to make it more challenging. It's nothing you can't figure out, but it is not very clean.

Overall, a good party game for 5-6. The box indicates that this is a game for ages 15+, and nothing in the content of the cards makes me think that anyone from age 7 and up can't handle.
text_fidelity_b: CGE Czech Games Edition Thats A Question

Winning Moves Games Pretty Princess Board Game I am a board game afficionado. I own over 200 different strategy, social or silly games, and you'd better believe that my daughter is a gamer in waiting. Of course, as a young boy, Pretty Pretty Princess wasn't on my radar for myself, but I knew the name and the concept, and when it was my time to find a copy for my kid, there's no way I was paying the multiple hundreds for the original 80's item.

So I was thrilled when an appropriately priced remake made it's way to my house, and all it took was reading the name to hook my daughter (and interestingly, my wife as well) into a quest to become the most beautiful in all the realm.

The box for this one opens upside down for some reason, and one you get inside, you'll find a spinner, an odd, nearly blank game board, and some teeny tiny jewels to bling out your ensemble. Play is simple - you spin the spinner, attempt to move aroudn the circular board to earn all your gems, and the first one to get everything is crowned (literally) the prettiest princess.

Perhaps the most striking thing is the lack of effort they put into the board and spinner. Both are of reasonable thickness and sturdy, but there is almost nothing on the board in terms of graphic design outside of the logo on the field of white, and the spinner is literally numbers. They may have changed the font away from Times New Roman, but that's all there is to it. It looks like a high school kid's graphic design project, and not one that's going to earn high marks from the teacher.

That said, it's good to have this game back in print again, even if the game play is not particularly solid, and even if the graphics leave quite a bit to be desired. As I said, all I needed to do to get my little one to play was to tell her the name of the game, and my wife jumped right in on the nostalgia boat as well.
text_fidelity_b: Winning Moves Games Pretty Princess Board Game

No, the fur doesn't really "shave off" it's more like you comb it off and grab it. It takes parental involvement and it's messy, but it's meant to be an experience, which it fully delivers. My daughter did the unboxing and loved finding all the surprises. We "shaved" her pup and gave it a bath in a bowl at my kitchen table. We set up a "drying station" with my hair dryer and a towel. The entire experience was magical and bonding for my daughter and I. We giggled and guessed if we would get the Frenchie or Yorkie and wondered what color it's nails would turn. Don't buy this toy if you can't be bothered to spend an hour playing with your child.
Don't buy this toy expecting a 5-7 year old to do this independently.
This toy is clearly meant for interactive play with an adult.
This toy was a wonderful addition to our homeschooling dramatic play for kindergarten.

If you want a toy that allows you and your child to pretend to own a grooming salon, this toy is perfect. Have everything prepared ahead of time. We put a table cloth down and a bowl of warm water with shampoo, then in a separate area we had the drying and grooming station. Expect to spend at least 45-60 minutes on this adorable experience. Crayola Aroma Putty, Silly Putty Alternative, Gift, 4 Count I am so glad I waited a few weeks to review this product -- When it first arrived, my reactions was little more than, "Hmm, that's interesting." I had the hardest time figuring out how to open the containers (they twist open), and the first few I opened had a very chemically, medicinal, almost artificial scent. Plus, I no longer subscribe to a daily newspaper, so the silly putty fun of my childhood -- copying pictures from the funny pages onto the putty -- was not really an option. Meh. It's okay. Kind of novel but not particularly useful.

I was headed to a funeral the next day, and I brought one of these along, thinking it might be a harmless diversion if I needed a little stress relief. I started with the peppermint. It smelled nice enough. Minty, a little bit chemical, but nice. Then I started to play with it, kneading it in my hand. At first, it was pretty hard, and I had to dig it out of the container. In no time, it became softer, just the right texture for kneading, stretching, twisting, wrapping around my finger, collapsing, kneading. It was kind of fun. I put it back in the container. My daughter opened each of the containers, stamping designs into the putty. The designs remained until the next time I opened the containers.

Since the funeral, I have had several IVs and blood draws. I brought along a little container of putty to the hospital, and found it worked just perfectly for the "make a fist and squeeze" stage. It was fun and distracting to play with while the IV was going. I keep a container in my purse, and find it fun to play with while riding the bus or subway, and when I need a whiff of something pleasant (as can happen when taking public transportation), I just hold the putty up to my nose. I can smell it, but the smell is not so strong or overwhelming as to bother others sitting nearby. And, as my husband discovered when he found a local high school newspaper, you can still copy comics from newsprint.

The containers are small and easily slip into a purse or backpack. So far, I haven't had any issues with the lids coming off when I don't want them to -- which often happens to things in my crowded purse. Occasionally, the putty becomes a little too warm and starts sticking to things. I was vigorously kneading it for some time and the putty started to stick under my rings. When that happened, I just put it away -- and it was back to its original texture in short course.

Overall, I'm really glad I discovered these little treats. They are an adult alternative to fidget spinners, and have provided more hours of -- I'm not sure if I'd call it pleasure or relief or what -- let's just say they have been used for many more hours than I ever expected I would use them, and the seem to be holding up well, staying good as new.
text_fidelity_b: Crayola Aroma Putty, Silly Putty Alternative, Gift, 4 Count

Loopdedoo – DIY Friendship Bracelet Maker Kit – Make Bracelets in Minutes – Award-Winning Craft Kit - Ages 8+ It's suggested for ages 8 and older, and I'd agree with that age range. I think younger kids could successfully use it if an older, experience person was nearby to help. Basically, you loop embroidery thread around the two hooks to create the desired core thickness, then twist a knob to spin the core while you lay down an outer design over that core. You tie on the finished piece using the end loops. The bracelet should withstand normal wear if tied according to the directions.

The distance from one hook to the other is 11", but longer items can be made by linking finished 11" pieces or by a somewhat trickier shifting of the piece after you have 11" of it's length finished. You can, of course, make lengths shorter than 11". The instructional book was easy to follow and was all I needed to create a nice bracelet with no frustration involved. They also have good instructional videos on their website: annwilliamsgroup. com/instructional-videos

Included in the kit is the main Loopdedoo tool (with a push-out drawer for storing the thread and clips); instructional booklet; 18 skeins of embroidery thread (100% cotton, 8.7 yards) in a variety of colors including reds through purples, black, brown, and cream; and 2 alligator clips (which are used with the tool to hold threads in place when making the longer items). The thread is Made in China, but I think the loop Loopdedoo is made in the USA.

I hope to use this tool with a group of middle grade girls soon as I think they'll get a kick out of it. The Loopdedoo is made from a solid plastic that feels like it will last. Is this fairly simplistic tool worth price? Well, if the person it's intended for will only make a few bracelets and then move on to the next toy, then probably not. But if she loves to make her own, unique bracelets and tends to continue with an activity she enjoys, then this might be a good tool to support her creativity.

text_fidelity_a:
Googly Eyes Game — Family Drawing Game with Crazy, Vision-Altering Glasses This game is FUN!
But may not be for kids that are perfectionist when art is involved.
The goggles have different settings - easy, medium, hard which makes it nice for the kids to start out with easy and adults to start at hard if your kids don't like losing.
The rules are easy.
This game is a fun "charades type" spin on a game.
The goggles make you look silly and is fun too!
This game is best for kids that are already pretty good artists, basically if they draw a lot with sidewalk chalk and you can really tell what they are drawing - then this will be good for them.
However, if your kids are still drawing stick people, then this is not the game for them, they will most likely leave the game crying.
I would consider 7 year olds as the very minimum, but I would base it more on the ability and less on age.
The kid should also be able to know how to read the simple instructions, which from my experience - 7 years is appropriate.
I think this game would be most fun for a group of kids the same age with the same artistic ability to really level the playing field. There is a possibility for cheating if you try looking at the end of the frame where the lense and frame meet. Hopefully nobody on your team decides to try that.
Keep an eye out for drawing with a head at an unexpected angle!
text_fidelity_b: Googly Eyes Game — Family Drawing Game with Crazy, Vision-Altering Glasses

LEGO Hidden Side Graveyard Mystery 70420 Building Kit, App Toy for 7+ Year Old Boys and Girls, Interactive Augmented Reality Playset (335 Pieces) I hope they don't overdo it, but this new LEGO Augmented Reality system is quite cool.

There is an app that you download to your phone, and using that app, you can view your LEGO set, and watch it move and change a little bit. If you've seen someone playing Pokemon Go or using a filter on their camera phone, you'll get the idea. It works surprisingly well given that it's easy to slightly alter the design. The app itself is downloadable on iTunes and Android, and works well on the Android system, although you really likely want to use a phone because of the size of the tablet. It will work, but it gets in the way of play.

Like all parents, I'm not entirely thrilled about yet another excuse to hand over my phone, but I think that the augmented reality piece is really more of a gimmick that my daughter will tire of sooner rather than later. The building of the set must come first in order for this to work, and that's mildly educational, and we get to play with the LEGO set without the phone as well.

And did I mention how cool this set is, even without the augmented reality? The ghost theme makes for some cool pieces, and I like how this one looks when it's done. It's a winner.

Monopoly Empire Game "Monopoly Empire" is like a simplified version of the traditional game of Monopoly. The colors and layout of the board are very similar to the traditional game, but each has a famous logo, such as Hasbro or EA Sports, instead of street names. The object of the game is to add tiles with various brands to your Times Square type "billboard tower" before the other players. The more brands you add to your billboard, the more money you get when passing Go, which allows you to buy more brands. The game tokens are representative of the brands in the game, such as a bottle of Coca-Cola and an Xbox controller. The board is a bit smaller than the traditional board, because it doesn't have railroads.

The game is easy to learn, in part because of an excellent, full-color instruction guide that includes a very clear diagram of how to set up the board. The way the items are priced make it easy to pay for purchased tiles. Although the game is lacking the excitement and strategy of trading properties and building houses as in the original version of Monopoly, it is good for a quick game. It would be easy for kids to learn and play. The game is most fun when it's a close race between the players to complete their towers. If one player takes a large, early lead, it's hard for the other person to come from behind.

Note: The logoed tiles have various sizes, which is part of the game. However, the sometimes the positioning of the stickers with the logo make it confusing to put them into the tower correctly.

All in all, this is a good game that is easy to play and goes by quickly.
text_fidelity_b: Monopoly Empire Game

HobbyZone Champ RTF, HBZ4900 This is a great little plane, no question. But I ignored Hobbyzone's recommendation for 14 years old and up. I bought two: one for each of my 9-year-old twin sons, who were hot to fly RC model airplanes. One learned to fly quickly, but the other has been seriously disappointed. And I had to learn quickly how to use styrofoam glue to reattach broken wings, tail parts, motor mounts, etc.

It took me a while to understand how critical the trim really is: a beginner really can't fly a plane that isn't trimmed properly. You can get the trim in the ballpark with visual inspection of the control surfaces, but to get it right you have to fly the plane yourself. When I did that, and touched up the trim, flying became a lot of fun - for one boy. The other boy still can't fly more than a few seconds before landing his plane on its nose. He has just about given up in disgust.

I suspect that in a year or two both boys will have good flying skills. But in the meantime one boy is ready to move up while the other is ready to give up. Bummer!
text_fidelity_b: HobbyZone Champ RTF, HBZ4900

Each deck is separated from the others with marked tabs. Each deck has 1 card that explains how best to use the cards to teach the concepts that relate to the math skills that they seek to teach and has suggestions for games and activities.

The Time cards show analog clocks on one side and the time in digital format on the other. The money cards show US currency, combinations of bills and coins, on one side and the value in numbers and words on the other. The fraction cards show circles divided into portions on one side and the value written in fraction format on the other side. The function cards have large numbers showing a problem and in smaller type the problem that is on the other side of the card, which makes it easier to quiz the child.

The flash cards themselves are each approximately twice the size of a regular deck of cards, but each set is still small enough to bring along.

text_fidelity_a:
Little Tikes Dozer Racer 2-in-1 Rc Vehicle for Kids UPDATE 10/10/18: The kids just love this RC car now that it works fine. It's frequently used by a 5-year-old boy and an 8-year-old girl, and it's holding up well to this heavy use. It is easy enough for the 5-year-old to work the controls, but entertaining enough for the 8-year-old to play with it with him. It doesn't run through the batteries as fast as I thought it would either.

UPDATE 9/18/18: I received the replacement toy, and it works perfectly. The toy is so fun and a good price for what you get. I wouldn't hesitate to buy one as a present in the future.

UPDATE 9/10/18: Yesterday (Sunday), I sent an e-mail to customer support about the malfunction. I received a reply early this morning. It was a real person who communicated clearly and actually addressed my problem. They're sending a replacement that has been tested to make sure it works fine. They're also sending a pre-paid return label for the return of the malfunctioning toy so their engineers can look at the unit. I'm super impressed.

ORIGINAL REVIEW (3 stars): This is generally such a fun, nice toy that I almost gave it 4 stars even though I would have returned this toy if I'd actually bought it. The remote is fairly simple: hold down the left button to turn left, hold down the right button to go right, hold both down to go forward. These button work great. But one of the transform buttons had a glitch from the beginning. The vehicle starts out as a race car when you turn it (and the remote) on. When you hit the bulldozer button, that transforms the race car into a bulldozer just fine every time. However, if the user likes to frequently switch back and forth between the two, the race car transform button will malfunction once out of every two or three times you hit it. When it malfunctions, instead of transforming into a race car, the bulldozer goes straight backward until it runs into something. Since there is no stop button, there is no way to stop the crash. You're no longer in control. At this point, the remote control commands do nothing, and you have to lift the vehicle to access the on/off switch to turn it off and on before it will work again. So far, it hasn't damaged the RC vehicle or anything else. However, this malfunction is a bother at the very least and will damage something eventually.

It's a cute toy that the kids really enjoy...as long as they don't transform often and crash every few minutes. The vehicle measures 10.5" long, 5.25" tall, and 7" wide. It requires 6 AA batteries--4 for the vehicle and 2 for the remote control. (Yes, we put brand new batteries in and tried another batch to see if the batteries were behind the problem. No improvement.) The toy is strong enough to push the box that it came in when in the bulldozer mode, and it can handle travel in a yard (at least when we tested it on a freshly mowed lawn). Intended for ages 3+. It certainly works well for the 5 year old boy who mainly plays with it. Made in China.
text_fidelity_b: Little Tikes Dozer Racer 2-in-1 Rc Vehicle for Kids

Earthtiles Wooden Magnetic Tiles by Big Future Toys - 100 Piece Set | Montessori Toys | Sensory Toys | Wooden Magnetic Blocks | STEM Building Toys | Wooden Blocks for Toddlers| Toddler Toys Age 3+ [[VIDEOID:2ed5b4ed724fe0fbfda0f1674e634e3d]] Good set of magnetic building shapes with a few thoughts. My kiddo was at a play-date recently, and the friend had a plastic set that the kids really enjoyed playing with. I saw these for review and thought they’d be a great addition to our play area at home. One thing I noticed right from the start is that they sound like baby rattles—you can really hear the magnets moving around inside as you move them. I didn’t notice this type of noise with the plastic ones at the play-date, so just something to keep in mind.

The wood is very smooth and each piece is lightweight. They appear to be durable as I don’t notice any bend if I put pressure on one of the pieces, but they also seem thin at the same time. I’m a little concerned that if someone steps on these by mistake, one of them could crack in half and expose little magnets everywhere. Up until this point, I’ve avoided a lot of toys with magnets, so I’m just going to have to be selective about when we play with these so I can really supervise how they’re being used.

Like magnets naturally do, sometimes the sides won’t link correctly if the positive and negative sides are connected right, so this is a normal learning curve for kids. Otherwise, they stand together very well and there’s plenty of pieces and shapes to build some neat things. These are very nice overall, and if you prefer wooden toys, these are a very good option.
